title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
summary_raw: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate
summary_raw: Consciousness researchers Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi argue in a Nature commentary that today's AI systems aren't conscious and won't become so on silicon hardware. They consider the assumption that consciousness depends on computation alone "fatally flawed" and warn against granting rights to AI systems. The article The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate appeared first on The Decoder .

title: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts
summary_raw: Turing Award winner Richard Sutton reaffirms that raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence and that fundamentally new learning methods are needed. Ex-OpenAI researcher Tworek agrees, saying blind transformer scaling "has reward hacked brains of a whole generation of scientists." A growing wave of startups is already betting on exactly this gap. title: AI coding agents still need human cleanup on nearly three out of four tasks in a real-world test
summary_raw: Alibaba's new coding-agent benchmark, Co-Design Bench, tests AI agents on real user requests that already tripped them up in practice. Even GPT-6 Astra, the top performer, fully solves only 26.4 percent of tasks. On older benchmarks, the same models score above 99 percent. title: Is AI Now Good Enough To Cure Cancer? | YC Paper Club
summary_raw: This week’s Paper Club is all about AI for biology. The cost of sequencing has collapsed, which means biology now generates more data than anyone can mine, and the models are finally catching up. We cover how falling sequencing costs are turning cancer care into a per-patient data problem, what it takes to model a cell rather than a molecule, what a language model trained on DNA actually learns, and why in-context learning showed up in a genome model that nobody trained for it.
